catalog_quote: [K&AK p.55] Assiuming [scan] that long vowels are treated as geminates, the stress rule accents the rightmost heavy syllable (except that CVC counts as light in final position) and otherwise the first syllable, without exceeding the antepenult. ... The rules formulated in (1) have been assumed as synchronic or diachronic processes in virtually all studies of Levantine dialectology. ... [p.64] the Beirut dialect does not have the accentual contrast between CaCaC versus CaaCaC and CaCCaC roots found in Tripoli and Ramallah. It uniformly stresses the second root syllable of feminine nouns amplified with a vowel-initial possessive suffix and thus respects an antepenultimate limit. ... In the Beirut dialect stress is assigned to the feminine perfect suffix -it regardless of the nature of the preceding root, as in Cairene Arabic. [McCarthy pp.78-79] A light syllable has the structure (5a) and a heavy syllable is one of (5b) or (5c). A third degree of weight -- superheavy -- is represented as (6a) or (6b). ... Stress falls on the penultimate syllable when it is heavy (7a) and in disyllables (7b). Otherwise stress falls on the antepenult (7c). Forms like muttahide 'united (f. sg.)' borrowed from Literary Arabic show that stress does not retract to the preantepenult even when the penult and the antepenult are light. Finally, the examples in (7d) display the characteristic stressing of a superheavy ultima.
sweep_summary: Seven title hits, two already the catalog's deciding sources (K&AK 1980, McCarthy 1980; re-read in the held SLS 10 scanned, and an open IDEALS copy of the volume was downloaded, though its text drops the K&AK p.55 paragraph). New open full text: Nasr 1959 (Phonetica 4: 89-94) via the archive.org Phonetica scan, a first-hand Beirut description whose Patterns 1-4 state exactly the catalog rule (rightmost heavy with final CVC light, else initial, antepenult limit in four-light-syllable words) and add secondary stress on other long syllables — confirms/refines, does not supersede K&AK. Chahal 2001 (Melbourne thesis) is intonation; PDF restricted to UniMelb logins, abstract silent on placement. Brame 1974 (LI 5) and Brame 1973 (Halle festschrift) are print/lending-only and concern Palestinian Arabic, whose rule K&AK already restate on p.55; Abu-Salim 1982 dissertation has no open copy (IDEALS lacks it) and is probably Palestinian too. catalog's classification stands as 'weight'; no contradiction found.

new_statements.reading: A 1959 first-hand description (author based in Beirut) of a Lebanese dialect: primary stress on the rightmost syllable whose vowel is followed by VV or two consonants in the string (equivalently the rightmost heavy syllable, with word-final CVC counting as light and final CVCC/CVVC as heavy); if there is none, initial stress in words of two or three light syllables and antepenultimate stress in words of four (examples [kamašítu], [sa?alítak]), i.e. never further left than the antepenult. Also reports secondary stress on the other long syllables ([Tàawúus], [sìžžàadáatna]) and a footnote that a second dialect keeps stress in place after -ha becomes -a (kamáša). Confirms the catalog's weight coding in every clause and refines its secondary-stress note ('none reported') with a report of secondary stress on non-primary long syllables.

new_statements.quote: The particular dialect that we investigated is Ammani-Jordanian Arabic, which has a stress pattern identical to Palestinian Arabic (van de Vijver, 1996). In this dialect, stress is said to usually fall on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable. It will fall on the penultimate if the penultimate syllable is heavy, as is shown in (1); otherwise it will fall on the antepenultimate syllable, as is shown in (2). The one complication to this pattern is that final syllables will bear stress if they contain a long vowel or have a final consonant cluster, as is shown in (3). (Bold indicates stress.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Ammani-Jordanian Arabic (stated to be identical in stress pattern to Palestinian Arabic): a final syllable is stressed if it is superheavy (long vowel, or final consonant cluster: darást, fakatábt, raaséen, hammaaméen); otherwise the penult if heavy, i.e. closed or with a long vowel (ʃáarak, ʔúrdon, máktabha, binsáameħ, saamáħatna); otherwise the antepenult (maʕállamak, fabárada, ʕallámatak). Stress therefore stays within the last three syllables and tracks weight, with final CVC not counting as heavy for the final-syllable clause. Instrumentally, stress correlates with longer duration, higher F1 and pitch accent placement, with effects smaller than in English.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No claim for this dialect. p. 4: 'Also, some analyses indicate the presence of secondary stress, while others do not.' The corpus words (four light syllables, antepenultimate stress) are not marked for secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions stated. p. 4 (general Arabic): 'The general pattern of stress placement in Arabic is that the last heavy syllable is typically stressed.' p. 20 (instrumental caveat): 'while stress effects and accent location do indicate the variable stress location described in phonological analyses, there is also a competing prominence with fixed location on the penultimate syllable' (penultimate lengthening; one of four speakers showed penultimate lengthening rather than stress lengthening phrase-finally).
new_statements.identity_note: de Jong & Zawaydeh 1999 describe Ammani-Jordanian Arabic (four female speakers recorded in Amman, 1997) and state its stress pattern is identical to Palestinian Arabic (citing van de Vijver 1996); both are South Levantine (sout3123). The existing catalog statement (Nasr 1959) is about Lebanese Arabic, which Glottolog classes under North Levantine, so de Jong & Zawaydeh is the first opened source for the South Levantine variety itself. Abu-Salim 1982 is, by title and the author's other work, on Palestinian Arabic, but was not opened.

new_statements.relation_note: The readable pages confirm the TYPE (quantity-sensitive, cyclic metrical assignment, bounded ternary foot = antepenult window, stress ordered before syncope/epenthesis), matching the catalog's weight coding from Kenstowicz & Abdul-Karim 1980 and the de Jong & Zawaydeh 1999 / Nasr 1959 statements held by the project; the placement rule itself (rightmost heavy syllable, final CVC light, else leftmost within the antepenult window) sits in the gated ch.3 (pp.58-111) and could not be checked, so this is agreement at outline level only, no refinement and no contradiction found.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the open pages the author states that Palestinian Arabic (PA) stress assignment refers to syllable weight (rime weight only; onsets irrelevant; heavy syllables attract stress), that metrical structure is assigned cyclically (Kiparsky 1979), that PA uses extrametricality (ch.3 sect.3.3 per TOC) and that the maximal foot in PA is ternary rather than unbounded, i.e. stress is confined to a bounded (three-syllable) window at the right edge. The explicit placement rule (which heavy syllable, default when no heavy syllable) is in ch.3 pp.58-111, which is behind the ProQuest login and was not read; the visible outline is fully compatible with the catalog's quantity-sensitive coding (rightmost heavy, else within the antepenult window) but does not itself state it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the open pages (pp.1-13); ch.3 not readable
new_statements.exceptions: open pages mention only that stressed-vowel shortening (ch.4 sect.4, pp.148-158) and syncope/epenthesis (ch.5) apply after metrical structure is erected and 'do not alter the underlying prominence relations' (printed p.5), i.e. opaque surface stress under syncope/epenthesis, consistent with the catalog quote from Kenstowicz & Abdul-Karim 1980 (stress precedes syncope and epenthesis)
new_statements.identity_note: Abu-Salim 1982 describes Palestinian Arabic ('PA'; p.1 'with special emphasis on Palestinian Arabic'), the author being a University of Jordan graduate; this is South Levantine Arabic (sout3123) directly, the same variety cluster as the catalog source (Kenstowicz & Abdul-Karim 1980, Levantine/Palestinian) and Abu-Salim 1980 SLS 10(2).

sources.quote: Jordanian Arabic (JA) is an example of a quantity-sensitive stress system where stress is assigned to a word-final super heavy (ʼSH) syllable made of a long vowel and a coda consonant, or a short vowel followed by two consonants. If no such syllable is at the end of a word, stress will fall on a heavy (ʼH) penult made up of a long vowel, or a short vowel followed by a consonant. Otherwise, stress will fall on the antepenultimate syllable by default. [p. 1] ... Stress is assigned to the rightmost superheavy (SH) syllable provided that it is not separated from the right edge of the word by more than two syllables, i.e., preantepenultimate syllables are never stressed in JA. In the absence of a (super)heavy syllable under the condition above, i.e., in the ultimate or penultimate syllable, the antepenultimate is stressed. [p. 2] ... All cases of opaque stress in this dialect involve an epenthetic vowel in the penultimate syllable or in the ultimate syllable in the two structures, respectively. [p. 1]

sources.quote: Stress in Arabic is predictable and quantity-sensitive (Altmann, 2006; de Jong & Zawaydeh, 1999) but may differ slightly across modern Arabic dialects (Watson, 2002). [...] Stress in Arabic usually falls on the heavy syllable comprising a long vowel, a diphthong or a short vowel nucleus followed by one or more consonants (syllables of the structure CVVC or CVCC, i.e., superheavy syllables which are longer than two moras). [...] In disyllabic words, stress falls on the penultimate syllable if the ultimate syllable is not heavy, as in /ðæ.ˈhæb/ 'gold'. In polysyllabic words, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable if it is heavy e.g., /jʊ.ˈnɑː.di:/ 'call' [...]; if not, then the antepenultimate syllable receives the stress as in /ʔæn.ˈfʊ.sæ.kʊm/ 'yourselves'. The stress falls on the first or last syllable when a word contains no heavy syllable, depending on the Arabic dialect. In some dialects, e.g., Jordanian, stress falls on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable (see de Jong & Zawaydeh, 1999).

sources.quote: 'In Arabic, stress assignment is determined by syllable weight. Lexical stress in Lebanese Arabic is described as falling on: a word-final superheavy syllable, then on a heavy penult, then for disyllabic words ending in CV or CVC, on the initial syllable, and otherwise on the antepenult, whether heavy or light (McCarthy 1979; Abdul-Karim 1980; Chahal 2001; Watson 2011). sources.note: weight-sensitive: superheavy ultima > heavy penult > antepenult, moraic trochees L>R with consonant and foot extrametricality, degenerate feet forbidden. Palestinian stresses the fourth mora from the right in four-light-syllable words (['shajaratun]) vs Beirut/Damascene ([sha'jaratun]) (Halle & Kenstowicz 1991). Epenthetic vowels are invisible to stress in Levantine and Iraqi; 'differential' vs 'non-differential' syncope (Cantineau 1939). Catalog cites Kenstowicz & Abdul-Karim 1980; consistent. Second-hand (McCarthy 1980, Hayes 1995, Halle & Kenstowicz 1991, Younes 1995, Cowell 1964).

Data was collected by the researchers over the past three years from many naturally occurring resources: live TV and radio programs, and everyday speech by Arab speakers, mainly in Jordan. [p. 15] ... Regarding stress, in 99% of the errors, the place and weight of the stressed syllable were intact. Some examples are given in (2) below.
